programme.title: Blue Planet 2
programme.desc: In Southeast Asia there is the so-calledThe Coral Triangle, an area containing the richest reef in the world.In this vibrant place, there is constant competition for space, food and a mate.Coral reefs, which cover less than 1/10 percent of the ocean floor, support 1/4 of known marine species.Corals create complex and diverse structures.Each reef also has a clearly marked boundary beyond which lies the ocean depth.It is a kind of wall that protects the city from waves.The reefs are inhabited by, among others:cuttlefish that prey on crabs.Although this crustacean's pincers pose a great threat, cuttlefish have an extraordinary weapon - their skin contains millions of pigment cells that create constantly changing patterns.Creatures that have adapted well to life in reefs that resemble underwater cities reap many benefits.

programme.title: Blue Planet 2: The Making of
programme.desc: Behind the scenes of the creation of a spectacular nature series that took 4 years to film.The teams implementing it visited all oceans.Thanks to the fact that the divers had the latest equipment, they could have very close encounters with the animals being filmed.Even in low light conditions, the cameras captured events invisible to the human eye.Inspection cameras show the lives of small creatures, and those equipped with a suction cup record what is happening in the ocean from the perspective of larger animals.Wanting to film the most extraordinary wildlife scenes, the team also visited coastlines in the farthest corners of the world, such as the Galapagos Islands.Marine life around these islands depends on cold currents feeding surface waters.

programme.title: The Boxing Day Tsunami
programme.desc: On December 26, 2004, the second day of Christmas, a devastating tsunami hit Indonesia and Thailand.It was the largest disaster of this type in history, and its dramatic effects were also felt in other parts of the world.It started with an earthquake under the Indian Ocean.A few minutes later, a hundred-meter wall of water broke through Indonesia.Then the tsunami reached Thailand, where it left unimaginable destruction in its wake.Scientists analyze the course of these tragic events and explain the connection between the earthquake and the subsequent tsunami.Rescuers give accounts of the fierce fight to save human lives, and survivors recall their losses in a tragedy that is difficult to recover from even after many years.

programme.title: Ancient Powers
programme.desc: The creators of the six-episode series, using advanced computer graphics, will present the history of the five most powerful civilizations of antiquity: Egypt, China, India, Rome and Greece.Ancient powers have a lot in common.In the fight for survival and domination, they went through similar stages of development.They conquered new territories, built societies and political systems, as well as formed cultures, developed trade, ideas and the art of war.Viewers will learn about the latest archaeological research on ancient powers.

programme.title: Asia: behind the scenes of production
programme.desc: Behind the scenes of a production about the fauna and flora of the largest continent on Earth.The series consists of seven episodes, and their creation took 2.5 thousand days.30 film teams were involved in the project.

programme.title: Seven Worlds, One Planet
programme.desc: Antarctica is the coldest and windiest continent.The climate here is harsh, and only the toughest can survive.From Weddell seals crushing the ice with their teeth, to colorful starfish covering the seabed hidden under the ice.Penguin chicks may lose their lives when confronted by killer whales and leopard seals.Meanwhile, starfish and huge worms line the seabed as a feeding spectacle takes place on the surface.Life comes to Antarctica because the ocean surrounding the continent is extremely rich.Thousands of penguins, seals, albatrosses and over a hundred huge whales feast on the krill schools.Unfortunately, the local waters are warming, and as the temperature increases, the future of the local fauna and flora looks more and more uncertain.
